extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and beginning graduate students in mathematical logic; researchers in logic
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the formal conditions (recursiveness, derivability conditions, and representability) and constructions (interpretations, pairing/β-functions, Chinese remainder) needed to prove Gödel's second incompleteness theorem and related representability/undecidability results in arithmetic and set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursively axiomatizable theory (set A recursive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory T is given by a recursive set A of axioms (i.e., the set of Gödel numbers of axioms is recursive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recursiveness is used to show the binary relation “d is the number of a deduction from A whose last component is a” is recursive, to choose a formula π(v1,v2) numeral-wise representing that relation in AE, and to define Prb_T(σ) = ∃v2 π(S⌜σ⌝, v2). The assumption is basic for formalizing provability and for the fixed-point constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Prb_T(σ) (provability predicate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prb_T(σ) is the sentence ∃v2 π(S⌜σ⌝, v2), where π numeralwise represents the recursive relation 'v2 codes a deduction from A whose last component is σ'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit construction of π depends on recursiveness of A; Prb_T is the arithmetical formula that formalizes 'T ⊢ σ' inside AE and is used throughout reflection, fixed-point, and Löb/Gödel arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivability condition 1: AE ⊆ T (reflection property externally)
rubrics_metrics.description: T includes AE (elementary arithmetic axioms), which via Lemma 37A gives: whenever T ⊢ σ then AE ⊢ Prb_T(σ), and if T includes AE then T satisfies external reflection T ⊢ σ ⇒ T ⊢ Prb_T(σ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures that the theory recognizes (externally) that its theorems are provable; needed as a base for formalizing reflection inside T and for applying fixed-point sentences asserting unprovability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivability condition 2: formalized reflection (Prb_T σ → Prb_T Prb_T σ)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any sentence σ, T proves (Prb_T(σ) → Prb_T(Prb_T(σ))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the reflection property within T itself. It is used to climb from 'σ is provable' to 'the provability of σ is provable' inside T, a key step in the formalized Lemmas and in deriving contradictions leading to Gödel's second theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivability condition 3: formalized modus ponens for provability predicate
rubrics_metrics.description: For any sentences ρ and σ, T proves (Prb_T(ρ → σ) → (Prb_T(ρ) → Prb_T(σ))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encodes modus ponens for the provability predicate inside T; combined with formalized reflection, it allows internal manipulation of provability statements and is necessary for Formalized Lemmas 37B/37C and Löb's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'sufficiently strong' theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory T is 'sufficiently strong' if it is recursively axiomatizable and meets the three derivability conditions: (1) AE ⊆ T, (2) T ⊢ (Prb_T σ → Prb_T Prb_T σ) for every σ, (3) T ⊢ (Prb_T(ρ→σ) → (Prb_T ρ → Prb_T σ)) for every ρ,σ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This composite criterion is precisely the hypothesis used to formalize the informal argument that leads to Gödel's second incompleteness theorem (and Löb's theorem). The textbook checks these conditions hold for standard theories like PA and for suitable formulations of set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-point (self-reference) sentence construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the fixed-point lemma to obtain a sentence σ with AE ⊢ (σ ↔ ¬Prb_T(σ)) (or more generally AE ⊢ (σ ↔ (Prb_T(σ) → τ))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction is required to produce the canonical 'I am unprovable' (or 'if I am provable then τ') sentences. The fixed-point sentence is the pivot of Lemma 37B/37C and of the proof that T cannot prove its own consistency unless inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation π of Cn(AE) into set theory ST — finite verification demands
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation π of the consequences of AE into ST must provide set-theoretic formulas π_∀, π_0, π_S, π_+, π_·, π_E etc. and satisfy (i) ∃v1 π_∀ ∈ ST, (ii) for each function symbol f in AE, ST contains the sentence asserting π_f defines a function on the set defined by π_∀, and (iii) for each sentence σ in AE, σ^π ∈ ST.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook explains how to embed number theory into set theory by representing numbers by sets (e.g., von Neumann ordinals), constructing π-translations of symbols, and checking a finite list of demands (which can be satisfied by a finite subset of ST). These demands justify transferring undecidability from arithmetic to set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong undecidability criterion for set-theoretic theories
rubrics_metrics.description: If T is a theory in the language of set theory such that T ∪ ST (or at least T ∪ a suitable finite subset of ST) is consistent, then the set of Gödel numbers of theorems of T is not recursive (i.e., T is not decidable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem (37D) is an application of the interpretation π and the nonrecursiveness of arithmetic: showing an interpretation of Cn(AE) into T yields a many-one reduction from arithmetic consequences to T's consequences, so T cannot be recursive if its arithmetic fragment is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of representability of exponentiation in AM (NM language)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a formula ε in the language of NM (AM axioms) such that for any a,b, AM ⊢ ∀z[ε(Sa0, Sb0, z) ↔ z = S(a^b)0], i.e., exponentiation is representable in Cn(AM).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To represent exponentiation without a primitive E symbol, construct an auxiliary decomposition function δ (Lemma 38A) and then define E**(a,b) as the least s with δ(s,0)=1 and for all i<b δ(s,i+1)=δ(s,i)·a; then ab = δ(E**(a,b), b). The proof depends on pairing functions, the β-function, and the Chinese remainder theorem to guarantee appropriate encodings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 38A: existence of decomposition function δ representable in Cn(AM)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a function δ representable in Cn(AM) such that for every n and sequence a0,...,an there exists s with δ(s,i)=ai for all i ≤ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text constructs δ via δ(s,i)=β(K(s),L(s),i) where K,L decode a pairing J(c,d) and β(c,d,i) is the remainder of c divided by 1+(i+1)·d. The lemma's proof uses Chinese remainder theorem together with Lemma 38B to produce suitable c,d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability of pairing functions J, K, L in Cn(AM)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist arithmetical functions J (pairing) and projections K, L such that J: N×N→N is bijective onto N and K(J(a,b))=a, L(J(a,b))=b, and J,K,L are representable in Cn(AM).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit formulas: J(a,b) = H((a+b)·(a+b+1)) + a with H(a) = least b such that a ≤ 2^b (or similar encoding as given); K(p) and L(p) as least witnesses. Showing these are definable in AM is part of coding sequences and necessary for β/δ constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and representability of Gödel β-function
rubrics_metrics.description: Define β(c,d,i) as the remainder in c ÷ [1 + (i + 1)·d], i.e., the least r with c = q·[1+(i+1)·d] + r for some q ≤ c. β is representable in Cn(AM) and used to decode sequences from a code pair (c,d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: β provides a practical decomposition; combined with pairing J to encode (c,d) into a single s, it yields δ(s,i)=β(K(s),L(s),i). Its construction is elementary number theory formalizable in AM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem prerequisites for sequence coding
rubrics_metrics.description: To encode arbitrary finite sequences as remainders, one needs moduli d0,...,dn that are pairwise relatively prime and numbers ai with 0 ≤ ai < di; then there exists c with remainders ai modulo di for all i ≤ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook invokes the CRT: choose d = s! and moduli 1+(i+1)·d (which are pairwise relatively prime by Lemma 38B) to ensure existence of c reproducing the target sequence via remainders; this is the key number-theoretic step in representability proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 38B: pairwise relative primality of 1+(i+1)·s!
rubrics_metrics.description: For any s ≥ 0, the s+1 numbers 1+1·s!, 1+2·s!, ..., 1+(s+1)·s! are pairwise relatively prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: any common prime factor q cannot divide s!, so q> s; if q divides both 1+j·s! and 1+k·s!, it divides their difference |j−k|·s!, thus divides |j−k| ≤ s, impossible unless j=k. This lemma ensures the chosen moduli for CRT are coprime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order relation comprehension validity
rubrics_metrics.description: For any formula ϕ in which the predicate variable Xn does not occur free, the second-order formula ∃Xn ∀v1...∀vn [Xn v1...vn ↔ ϕ] is valid (relation comprehension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a semantic principle of full second-order logic: one can quantify over relations and assert existence of exactly the relation defined by ϕ. It is used to state categoricity results (e.g., Peano axioms with second-order induction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order function comprehension validity
rubrics_metrics.description: If ψ is a formula not containing the function variable Fn free, and ∀v1...∀vn ∃!vn+1 ψ holds, then ∃Fn ∀v1...∀vn+1 (Fn v1...vn = vn+1 ↔ ψ) is valid (function comprehension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to relation comprehension; guarantees existence of a function symbol corresponding to any definable functional relation, underpinning expressive power of second-order logic and categorical characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order Peano induction yields categoricity
rubrics_metrics.description: The second-order induction axiom ∀X(X0 ∧ ∀y(Xy → XSy) → ∀y Xy), together with basic successor axioms S1,S2, implies any model is isomorphic to (N;0,S); i.e., the set of these second-order sentences is categorical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard result: full second-order induction quantifies over all subsets and rules out nonstandard models, unlike first-order induction. The textbook highlights this as a motivation for second-order logic's greater expressive strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order characterization of well-ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation is a well-order iff the second-order sentence ∀X(∃y Xy → ∃y(Xy ∧ ∀z(Xz → y ≤ z))) holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a second-order sentence that expresses the 'every nonempty subset has a least element' property; it is an example of how second-order quantification captures set-level properties not expressible in first-order logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order sentences characterizing infinite domains
rubrics_metrics.description: There are second-order sentences (e.g., λ_∞) equivalent to 'the domain is infinite', for example ∃X[∀u∀v∀w(Xuv → Xvw → Xuw) ∧ ∀u¬Xuu ∧ ∀u∃vXuv] or ∃F[∀x∀y(Fx=Fy→x=y) ∧ ∃z∀x Fx ≠ z].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These second-order characterizations show second-order logic can distinguish finiteness/infinite-ness categorically, which implies failure of compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem for second-order logic; the textbook uses them to demonstrate semantic differences from first-order logic.
